research_text:
## 1. API and finding

`javax.crypto.KeyGenerator` generates symmetric `SecretKey` objects. `getInstance` selects a key-generation algorithm, optionally with a provider; `init` configures the generator; and `generateKey()` returns a key. The reported `HmacSHA1` value concerns the **algorithm argument to `getInstance`**, not a reported key size or the MAC operation itself. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html))

Java documents `HmacSHA1` as a supported standard algorithm; its presence in the Java API is distinct from its exclusion by this CrySL rule. The finding alone does not establish which provider, initialization arguments, generated-key consumers, or persisted artifacts are involved. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html))

Source: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html`

## 2. Documented usage and guidance

Oracle recommends **explicit initialization**, because provider defaults can differ or change. Initialization can specify a key size, algorithm-specific parameters, and/or a `SecureRandom`, depending on the overload. Unsupported key sizes or inappropriate parameters can produce documented exceptions; no invalid size can be inferred from this finding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html))

Oracle’s JCA guide demonstrates generating an `HmacSHA256` key and initializing a separately obtained `HmacSHA256` `Mac` with it. Changing the generator alone does not change the separately selected `Mac` algorithm. The API documentation does **not** prescribe a finding-specific remediation for using `HmacSHA1`. Separately, NIST recommends transitioning federal applications away from SHA-1 toward SHA-2 or SHA-3, while recognizing that historical information may still need SHA-1 processing. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

Sources: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html`; `https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/hash-functions/nist-policy-on-hash-functions`

## 3. Compatibility and migration limits

- **Platform support:** Java SE 21 requires `HmacSHA256` and `HmacSHA1`; Java SE 27 also requires both. Support for other algorithms and sizes must be checked against the actual platform and provider. For example, SE 21 lists AES-128 as required, whereas SE 27 lists AES-128 and AES-256. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Names:** Java standard algorithm names are case-insensitive. The CrySL file itself does not explain how a detector handles case or aliases. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
- **Persisted and wire formats:** `KeyGenerator` does not define an application’s storage or wire format, nor an automatic migration path for existing keys or authentication tags. A change to the MAC algorithm must be considered against the actual consumers and protocol: for example, RFC 4868 specifies protocol-specific HMAC-SHA-2 algorithms and truncation for IPsec, not a universal Java migration procedure. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html))

Sources: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html`; `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html`; `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4868`

## 4. Matching rule in the cited CrySL file

The file declares `SPEC javax.crypto.KeyGenerator`. Its **verbatim acquisition-event clause** is: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyGenerator.crysl))

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;
```

It declares `algorithm` as `java.lang.String` and constrains it to `AES`, `HmacSHA256`, `HmacSHA384`, or `HmacSHA512`. Thus the file shows one- and two-argument `getInstance` event forms—not an unrestricted parameter list. It also declares `init` forms with one or two arguments and `generateKey()` with none; its order is `Get, Init?, GenKey`. For AES, it states a key-size constraint of 128, 192, or 256, requires `randomized[random]`, and ensures `generatedKey[key, algorithm]`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyGenerator.crysl))

**A name alone is not a rule declared for an unrelated receiver type:** the file specifies `javax.crypto.KeyGenerator`. However, the file does not itself define an analyzer’s method-resolution implementation, so it cannot establish how a particular detector handles an unrelated same-named method. It also does not explain the extra alias spellings in the supplied detector message or how an unbound `keysize` is evaluated. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyGenerator.crysl))

Source: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyGenerator.crysl`
